meta.framing: How do investigators determine whether a worker's injury by an industrial robot arm stemmed from a defect in its control software or from the worker's bypassing of a safety interlock, when the manufacturer and the employer each blame the other?

response:
When an industrial robot injures a worker and the manufacturer and employer each blame the other, investigators set aside both narratives and rebuild the sequence of events from physical, electronic, and documentary evidence. The first step is to fix provenance and chronology. RoboDyne manufactured the industrial robot arm involved in the injury, and that manufacture predates the later moment when the worker was struck by the robot arm while inside its operating cell. Establishing this order defines the boundaries of the inquiry. It covers the design and software the arm carried from the factory, together with the configuration, maintenance, and workplace practices that came afterward.

The second step is to classify the outcome, because the severity of the harm determines the investigating authority, the evidentiary standards, and the legal exposure of each party. Either the injured worker survived the incident or the injured worker died from the injuries caused by the robot arm. The two outcomes cannot both be true, and one of them must hold. The medical examiner determined that the injured worker died from the injuries caused by the robot arm. In this inquiry, the fatal outcome is treated as what caused the strike inside the cell, so the matter proceeds as a fatality investigation. The parties' positions then frame the technical questions. RoboDyne argued that the worker had bypassed the safety interlock, whereas the employer argued that a defect in the control software caused the arm to move unexpectedly. These positions are not merely rhetorical. Each one points investigators toward a different body of evidence, the gate hardware in one case and the controller code in the other.

Investigators therefore do not begin by assuming that the two explanations exclude each other. At least one of two technical facts must hold, perhaps both: the robot arm's control software contained a defect, or the worker had bypassed the safety interlock on the cell gate. Industrial accidents frequently combine latent design flaws with unsafe work practices, so a finding on one branch does not by itself clear the other. Electronic records are usually central to separating them. Investigators downloaded the robot controller's event logs after the injury. By contrast, the controller event logs had been erased before investigators arrived. This leaves the electronic record unable to resolve the dispute alone, and it shifts weight onto configuration data and physical examination of the cell.

The configuration record is precise. The robot controller was running firmware version 4.2 at the time of the injury. That is, version 4.2 of the firmware was installed and active on the robot controller when the injury occurred. Pinning down the exact version allows engineers to compare the arm's recorded behaviour against the documented motion logic of that build. It also lets them test whether any known fault in that build could produce the reported movement. The 4.2 firmware in turn led directly to the decisive physical finding at the gate: investigators found a jumper wire attached across the interlock switch terminals. That wire confirms the bypass of the gate interlock, because a jumper across those terminals tells the controller that the gate is closed when it is in fact open. RoboDyne had issued a recall of the controller software two years before the injury. On its face, such a recall supported the employer's account.

The review board's determination settled the dispute. The review board concluded that the bypassed interlock, not a software defect, was the cause of the injury. The board weighed a documented software history against direct physical proof of tampering at the safety device. It gave controlling weight to the hardware evidence, because the jumper wire accounted for the worker's presence inside a live cell regardless of any flaw in the code. The general method follows from this reasoning. Investigators fix chronology, classify the outcome, and frame the competing accounts as non-exclusive possibilities. They then test each one against configuration records and physical traces, and they allow the evidence that most directly explains the hazardous exposure to govern the finding of cause.
